analysis.one_liner: Phases out ozone-destroying CFC chemicals by 1996 and bans imports from countries without matching phaseouts.
analysis.headline: The ozone phaseout bill drew 159 cosponsors from both parties but never got a vote; in May 1990 the record pointed to H.R. 3030, which became the broader 1990 Clean Air Act overhaul.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Clean Air Act to freeze production of ozone-depleting chemicals like CFCs and halons at 1986 levels, cut them in half by 1993, and ban their production for most uses by 1996 — a faster schedule than the Montreal Protocol treaty required. It would also have barred imports of these chemicals and of products made with them from countries without equivalent phaseout programs, required recycling of refrigerants, and forced warning labels on products containing the chemicals. The bill was referred to two committees, received a subcommittee hearing, and never came to a floor vote; its subject matter was taken up in H.R. 3030 later the same year.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people exposed to ultraviolet radiation. The bill's own findings state that ozone depletion increases skin cancer, cataracts, and potentially immune suppression, and that the treaty's slower schedule would let ozone-depleting chemicals keep building up in the atmosphere at an unacceptable rate [S2][S3]. Faster elimination of CFCs and halons would lower those risks, and recycling rules would also reduce these gases' contribution to climate change [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Freezes production of CFCs and halons at 1986 levels within 180 days, halves it by mid-1993, and bans production for anything other than medical purposes from July 1996 [S2][S3]
Requires a 95 percent cut in total ozone depletion potential by 1997, with the ban kicking in automatically if EPA fails to write the rules [S2][S3]

Bars imports of these chemicals and products made with them unless the exporting country runs a program at least as strict as the U.S. phaseout, and blocks U.S. investment in new CFC plants abroad [S2][S3]

Requires certified recycling equipment and trained technicians for car air conditioner service, service ports on new appliances so refrigerant can be recovered, and warning labels on containers and products [S2][S3]

analysis.who_pays: Chemical companies producing CFCs and halons would lose a product line, and the industries that use them — aerosols, solvents, foam blowing, refrigeration and air conditioning — would bear redesign, recycling-equipment, and certification costs, some of which would show up in prices for appliances and car repairs [S3]. Small auto-repair shops servicing fewer than 100 air conditioners a year got a one-year delay [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: CFC makers and industries using them

drawbacks.text: The phaseout ran ahead of the Montreal Protocol schedule the U.S. had already agreed to, so the transition to substitutes would have been compressed, with compliance costs for appliance makers, repair shops, and eventually consumers [S2][S3]
Import bans and investment prohibitions tied to country-by-country EPA certification would have raised prices for imported goods and invited trade friction with nations outside the agreement [S3]

Small service businesses would have had to buy certified recycling equipment and put technicians through certification, a real fixed cost even with the extra year for shops under 100 services a year [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health case was strong — the bill's own findings describe skin cancer and cataract increases from ozone loss and call no level of depletion safe [S3] — and the costs, while real for chemical producers and equipment-using industries, were one-time transition costs of moving off a product the science had condemned. The main honest criticism is pacing: the bill demanded a faster phaseout than the international treaty or, arguably, the substitute-chemical supply of 1989 guaranteed, which would have concentrated transition costs on U.S. producers and repair businesses before alternatives were fully available.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in two House committees, got one subcommittee hearing in January 1990, and in May 1990 the record simply pointed to H.R. 3030 — its ozone subject was folded into the broader Clean Air Act rewrite instead of moving on its own.

narrative.text: Introduced June 21, 1989, and referred jointly to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees [S1][S5]
Referred to subcommittees on Trade, Health and the Environment, and Commerce, Consumer Protection and Competitiveness; a subcommittee hearing was held January 25, 1990 [S5]
On May 23, 1990, the action record states 'For Further Action See H.R. 3030' — no committee ever reported the bill and no vote was ever taken on it [S5]

H.R. 3030 was the vehicle for the Clean Air Act Amendments of 1990, which became law later that year and included the stratospheric ozone provisions that had been building through this period (widely reported)

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never moved, CFC and halon producers avoided the strictest version of the phaseout — a 1996 near-ban and a 1997 95 percent cut — that this bill demanded; the eventual 1990 Clean Air Act law set a slower schedule. The broader public still ended up with a phaseout when the omnibus law passed, but the faster timeline this bill's 159 cosponsors backed never came to a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: CFC producers, who got a slower phaseout

for.name: Rep. Jim Bates
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Stratospheric Ozone Protection Act of 1989 on June 21, 1989

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill; referred it to subcommittees, held one hearing, and pointed the record to H.R. 3030 instead

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Trade Subcommittee on June 28, 1989, where it stayed with no further action

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was heavily bipartisan in raw terms — 142 of 257 Democrats and 17 of 175 Republicans signed on — though Democratic support was proportionally broader.

industries.note: The bill froze their production at 1986 levels, cut it in half by 1993, and banned most production by 1996 — eliminating their core product line on a schedule faster than the Montreal Protocol. Their interest in continuing unrestricted sales ran directly against the public's interest in limiting ozone loss.

industries.industry: Aerosol, solvent, and foam manufacturers using CFCs
industries.note: Small pressurized containers would be banned from interstate commerce after 1990 and virgin CFC use as solvents and blowing agents cut at least 50 percent within three years. Continued reliance on cheap CFCs came at the ozone layer's expense.

industries.industry: Refrigeration and air conditioning appliance makers
industries.note: New appliances would need service ports to recover refrigerant, adding design costs, but the substitute-chemical mandates created a guaranteed market for redesigned, lower-risk products. Gains and losses roughly offset.

Shops servicing car air conditioners would have to buy certified recycling equipment and certify technicians, a real fixed cost; shops under 100 services a year got a one-year delay, and recovering refrigerant also protects the public's atmosphere.
Mandating safe alternatives and a phaseout timetable creates customers for replacement chemicals and recycling equipment. Their gain comes alongside the public's gain from reduced emissions.
